Nāṭyaśāstra
(‘science of dramaturgy’)
------------------------------------------
Drama, dance and मुसिच् have been a very ancient and important aspect of हिन्दु चुल्तुरे. These three together have been dealt with as a common discipline under the name ‘nāṭyaśāstra’.
The earliest systematic treatment of this subject is contained in the Nāṭyaśāstra of भरत who might have lived during the 2nd or the 3rd century A. D. Nothing is known of him.
The work probably had 6000 ślokas or verses distributed in 36 chapters. It has a well-known commentary Abhinava-bhāratī of अभिनवगुप्त which, however, is available only in fragments. Other writers known to have commented upon it are: Bhaṭṭanāyaka, Harṣa, Kīrtidhara, Lollaṭa, Mātṛguptācārya, Śaṅkuka and Udbhaṭa.
None of these, however, is available now.
The main subject of this work is dramaturgy. भरत names ten forms of drama (Daśarūpaka). He also develops the theory of रस in poetics. Figures of speech like upamā (comparison or simile), rūpaka (metaphor), dīpaka (enlightener) and yamaka (same word with double meaning) are enumerated by him. He also narrates ten guṇas (excellences), ten doṣas (defects) and thirty six lakṣaṇas (characteristics) of a poetical composition.

Naṭarāja
(‘king of dance or dancers’)
------------------------------------------
Śiva, देवी and विष्णु are the three aspects of the Supreme Lord, most commonly worshipped by the Hindus even today.
Though शिव is generally worshipped in the temples in the aniconic form, the लिङ्ग, iconic forms are not uncommon. They are mostly depicted on the walls and niches outside the sanctum.
These iconic forms are generally divided into eight categories (See ŚIVA for details.) of which Nṛtta or Tāṇḍava mūrtis are also one. Treatises on dancing describe 108 modes of dancing, all attributed to शिव as the originator.
However, out of the nine modes more well-known and popular, the नटराज aspect is the best.
The earliest use of the name ‘Naṭarāja’ appears in the Kārikās of Nandikeśvara on the Māheśvarasūtras of पाणिनि (400 B. C.). There he mentions that शिव sounded his डमरु (small sounding drum) fourteen times at the end of his dance, producing fourteen sound-patterns —which are now called Māheśvarasūtras —like a i uṇ and so on, which form the basic structure of entire Sanskrit grammar.
The earliest idea of शिव as a dancer can be traced to the Śivasūtras (3.9-11), a cardinal text of Kashmir शैविस्म्.
The नटराज icon shows him with four hands and two legs, in the posture of dancing. There is the डमरु (drum) in the upper right hand and fire in the left. The lower right hand is in abhayamudrā (pose of protection) and the left is pointing towards the uplifted left foot. The right foot is resting on the demon अपस्मार-पुरुष. The whole image may be surrounded by a circle of blazing fire.
Śiva’s dance indicates a continuous process of च्रेअतिओन्, preservation and destruction. The डमरु represents the principle of शब्द (sound) and hence आकाश (ether), which proceeds immediately from the आत्मन् and is responsible for further च्रेअतिओन् or evolution. Fire represents pralayāgni, the fire that destroys the world at the time of dissolution of the world, and hence symbolises the process of destruction. Thus डमरु and fire represent the continuous cycle of च्रेअतिओन्, preservation and destruction. The other two hands indicate that he who takes refuge at the feet of the Lord will have nothing to fear. The अपस्मार-पुरुष (Apasmāra = epilepsy) symbolises इग्नोरन्चे which makes us lose our balance and चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्. He is trampled upon by the Lord for the good of the devotees who take refuge.
